en: For those who postulate that a universal (sāmānya) is all-pervasive, eternal, and unitary,
its non-existence is established here in order to sever the knot of delusion.

How is this understood—that among momentary entities perceived as mutually distinct through direct perception, a persisting form (*anuyāyirūpa*) which serves as the basis for the production of non-different cognitions and verbal expressions is not accepted by the wise? We reply: because of the absence of any proving evidence (*sādhaka-pramāṇa*) and the presence of subverting evidence (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*). For instance, regarding the moments characterized as such, that inference which is propounded by others as a proof for the existence of a universal (*sāmānya*)— [The opponent’s argument: "That which, being present in many things, does not exist without them, is their universal; for example, the nature of 'cowness' is the universal of cows. [The response: This is not so. Because it is not established that it exists in many things. For even if one were to say, "It exists in all cows," since the subject (*dharmin*) is not established, the reason (*hetu*) would be unestablished (*asiddha*). Furthermore, if one says, "It exists in some cows," then the reason would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because it would also apply to those things with which it is not identical, such as the universal of "existence" (*sattāsāmānya*). Moreover, if one says, "It exists in all individual cows (*vyakti*)," then the reason would be contradictory (*viruddha*), because the property of existing in all individuals is incompatible with the nature of a universal. Furthermore, if one says, "It exists in all cows without exception," then the reason would be unestablished, because the subject—the collection of all cows—is not established. Therefore, the reason is unestablished. Moreover, if one says, "It exists in all cows without exception, because it is a universal," then the reason would be inconclusive, as it would also apply to the universal of "existence" and so forth. Furthermore, if one says, "It exists in all cows without exception, because it is the object of the cognition 'this is a cow'," then the reason would be contradictory, because the property of being the object of the cognition 'this is a cow' is incompatible with the nature of a universal. Furthermore, if one says, "It exists in all cows without exception, because it is the cause of the cognition 'this is a cow'," then the reason would be unestablished, because the subject—the collection of all cows—is not established. Furthermore, if one says, "It exists in all cows without exception, because it is the object of the cognition 'this is a cow' which is produced by the power of the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of repeated experience," then the reason would be inconclusive, because it would also apply to the universal of "existence" and so forth. Furthermore, if one says, "It exists in all cows without exception, because it is the cause of the cognition 'this is a cow' which is produced by the power of the impressions of repeated experience," then the reason would be contradictory, because the property of being the cause of the cognition 'this is a cow' produced by the power of the impressions of repeated experience is incompatible with the nature of a universal. Furthermore, if one says, "It exists in all cows without exception, because it is the cause of the cognition 'this is a cow' which is produced by the power of the impressions of repeated experience and is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpodha*)," then the reason would be unestablished, because the subject—the collection of all cows—is not established. Furthermore, if one says, "It exists in all cows without exception, because it is the cause of the cognition 'this is a cow' which is produced by the power of the impressions of repeated experience, is free from conceptual construction, and is non-erroneous (*abhrānta*)," then the reason would be inconclusive, because it would also apply to the universal of "existence" and so forth. Furthermore, if one says, "It exists in all cows without exception, because it is the cause of the cognition 'this is a cow' which is produced by the power of the impressions of repeated experience, is free from conceptual construction, is non-erroneous, and is produced by the power of the impressions of repeated experience," then the reason would be contradictory, because the property of being the cause of the cognition 'this is a cow' produced by the power of the impressions of repeated experience, being free from conceptual construction, being non-erroneous, and being produced by the power of the impressions of repeated experience is incompatible with the nature of a universal. Furthermore, if one says, "It exists in all cows without exception, because it is the cause of the cognition 'this is a cow' which is produced by the power of the impressions of repeated experience, is free from conceptual construction, is non-erroneous, is produced by the power of the impressions of repeated experience, and is not produced by the power of the impressions of repeated experience," then the reason would be unestablished, because the subject—the collection of all cows—is not established. Furthermore, if one says, "It exists in all cows without exception, because it is the cause of the cognition 'this is a cow' which is produced by the power of the impressions of repeated experience, is free from conceptual construction, is non-erroneous, is produced by the power of the impressions of repeated experience, is not produced by the power of the impressions of repeated experience, and is produced by the power of the impressions of repeated experience," then the reason would be inconclusive, because it would also apply to the universal of "existence" and so forth. Whatever cognition possesses a corresponding form is based upon an object possessing that same form, as for example, the cognition "garland" regarding many flowers. However, there exists a cognition with a corresponding form regarding individual effects and so forth, which are devoid of mutual conjunction; because its body is beset by the flaw of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*), it is not capable of proving the existence of that [universal].
Since, among many cooks, there arises a conceptual cognition (*parāmarśapratyaya*) of a single form such as "cook, cook," yet no single entity (*vastu*) exists that is common to them— otherwise,
the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of such a cognition arising even before [the actual observation] would be unavoidable.
If it is argued that this fault does not apply because the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), which depend on assistance through action, manifest the universal, this is not so.
For eternal things, since no excellence can be imparted to them, dependence upon auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) is impossible, as they cannot be assisted.
Alternatively, if excellence were to be imparted, their nature would be such that they perish at every moment; thus, from where could action arise? This fault is difficult to avoid.

The claim that there is no fault of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) because the inclusive cognition (*anugatākāra-pratyaya*) regarding cooks is based on their action (*kriyā*) is also trivial; for it is impossible for actions—which differ with each individual—to be the basis for such a cognition.
If distinct things could indeed serve as the basis for a non-distinct cognition, then the existence of individuals themselves in that same manner would not be barred by the king’s rod of punishment.

Consequently, by adopting a position that strikes at the very root of his doctrine— that the universal (*sāmānya*) must not be admitted— the "Beloved of the Gods" (the Fools) has acted most effectively against himself; for by this same logic, he rejects the notion of a recurring cognition among cooks based on the commonality of the act of cooking, while instead postulating that the relationship between action and its factors (*kriyākārakasambandha*) is grounded in a single, non-differentiated cognition.
Therefore, one should not think that there is the fault of inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatā);
for a genus (jāti) connected with one thing is not the cause for the arising of a cognition of another thing, as that would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
This might be argued:

"By the force of the relation of inherence-in-the-inherent (samavetasamavāya), the universal of the action of cooking produces a reflective cognition (*parāmarśapratyaya*) of a non-differentiated form with respect to the cooks;
therefore, the aforementioned fault does not apply.
This too is without substance.

Since actions themselves are impossible because they perish immediately after their arising, when an action has perished, its universal cannot reside in that action due to the action's absence; nor can it reside in the agent. Thus, even by way of a "connected-to-a-connection" (saṃbaddha-saṃbandha), it does not exist [in the agent], and so it is not the cause of a non-differentiated cognition.

Therefore, it is established that because it is vitiated by the fault of being inconclusive (anaikāntika), this inference is not sufficient to prove the existence of a universal. This is what was stated [by the opponent] with the words "because it is devoid of... (°varjitayā).
For this reason as well, this inference does not establish a universal existence (*sāmānya-sattā*).

Just as entities such as brindled cows (*śābaleya*), though possessing mutually distinct natures, assist that single intended uniform form by means of a certain inherent nature—arisen from the power of their own causes—which is characterized by a restriction to that single effect, and which exists without another intervening universal (lest there be an infinite regress), so too may they produce a single synthetic cognition (*parāmarśa-pratyaya*). Why, then, accept an intervening, redundant universal that possesses a separate existence? That single [cognition]...
Now it is said: all entities possess specific, restricted potencies,
and this must necessarily be admitted even by those who deny the existence of universals.

Otherwise, when faced with the objection—"Why does a rice seed produce only a rice sprout and not a *kodrava* sprout?"—what else remains to be said here besides the "nature of things" (*bhāvaprakṛti*)? This answer is not devoured by the forest-dwellers (the Buddhists) either;
for we too are indeed capable of saying this.

"Even though there is no difference in their individuality (*bheda*), it is the universal alone that is capable of assisting [the production of] the individuals, yet it does not produce that single cognition;
alas, what an unsurpassed thicket of faults this is! Your Honor, though being led into it by the fault of your own vision, does not perceive yourself by yourself.

For instance, once the causal relation between a rice seed and its sprout has been understood—based on perception and non-perception—it can be stated that the rice seed is capable of producing a rice sprout, but not a *kodrava* sprout."

The relationship of beneficiary and benefactor between the universal and its possessor has not been established by any means of valid cognition; therefore, how can this answer being stated possess any merit? Enough with this futile persistence! It is not merely due to the absence of a proving cognition that the wise engage in the conventional usage of "non-existent.
Consequently, let us consider the inference we have stated which establishes that very non-existence.
Having entered [the discussion],
those who possess discernment should treat as non-existent whatever, being characterized by perceptibility, is not perceived.

Just as a lotus in the sky is not perceived, so too a universal (*sāmānya*) is not perceived anywhere, even though it meets the conditions for perception; this is a non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*).
One should not object here by raising the fault of the reason being unestablished (*asiddha*).

For instance, if there were non-establishment (*asiddhi*) here, would it occur by way of its own nature (*svarūpa*) or by way of its qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*)? In that regard, the first [alternative] is not possible, because non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) is admitted to be of the nature of the apprehension of another,

and since its own nature is directly realized through self-cognizing perception (*svasaṃvedanapratyakṣa*), how could there be any room for the fault of non-establishment by way of its own nature?° First.

Now it may be argued that self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) is simply not possible, because of the contradiction of an action upon itself: for a blade cannot cut that very same blade by its own edge, nor can a fingertip touch that very same fingertip with itself;
therefore, this reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*).
This very statement merely reveals the manifestation of a failure to understand the meaning of the term *svasaṃvedana* (self-cognition).
For instance,
a cognition arises that is excluded from [the categories of] jar, silver, blue lotus, and so forth.
Therefore, its very arising in the form of consciousness is called self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*), like light; for there is no relation of object, agent, and action,
since it is impossible for a single, partless entity to possess a threefold nature.

For just as light, being manifest while independent of any other illuminator, is said to be the illuminator of itself, so too knowledge, being manifest while independent of another knowledge, is said to be the illuminator of itself. Therefore, this is the ultimate truth:
it is not logical that knowledge should be cognized by another knowledge, nor is it said to be uncognized.

Furthermore, when the intended meaning of the term *svasaṃvedana* (self-cognition) is understood as "in the manner [of its own]," there is nothing at all that remains to be said; how, then, could there be any occasion for the aforementioned fault? Nor is it the case that a failure due to the non-establishment of the qualification (*viśeṣaṇāsiddhi*) should be raised as a point of contention.
Since the universal itself is accepted by others as meeting the conditions for apprehension (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*),
or else— if it were not so accepted— cognition and verbal expression with a recurring form would not occur in respect to Bāhuleya and other individuals by virtue of that universal;

for when the occurrence of cognition and naming proceeds from something toward something else, there can be no apprehension of that [latter] without the perception of the former, just like [the perception of] a staff.

Or, regarding the [logical reason] "because it is perceived" (*upalambhāt*) in the context of the family-lineage (*kuleya*), as for this which has been illuminated by Uddyotakara: do you admit a universal (*sāmānya*) or not? If you admit it, how can you deny it? But if you do not admit it, then because that [universal] is unestablished (*asiddha*), the reason (*hetu*) suffers from the fallacy of having an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddha*).

This appears to be a manifestation of ignorance regarding the true nature of that subject (*dharmin*), because we do not accept the universal (*sāmānya*) as the subject by way of an external form. Rather, it is employed as the subject because it consists of a form of cognition (*jñānākāra*) superimposed upon an external object—which arises from the maturation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) produced by the presence of both existence and non-existence, or neither—residing solely within the internal [mind].
And since this is established by the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*), it cannot be rejected. (S)
Because of the departure from that which was deposited by experience, those who are established regarding this subject (*dharmī*) deliberate upon its existence or non-existence:

"Is this subject, which appears as the object of a conceptual construction involving a general term, based on an external universal imagined by others? When it is not based on an external [object], non-apprehension is the reason, insofar as it is the probandum.
Furthermore, it is not the non-existence of that very [subject] which is being established, because that would entail the consequence of not employing words whose referent is that subject.
And when such a subject (dharmin) is intended to be expressed, how could there be the fault of the unestablished locus (āśrayāsiddhi)? Is it likewise [unestablished] in the probandum (sādhya)?

As for what is said—that because its nature is established by the means of valid cognition of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), this reason is unestablished—that is incorrect, because it does not appear in its own form.
For this indeed is the perceptibility of direct perception: that it presents its own form to its own cognition.
This universal (*sāmānya*), however, is like one who buys without paying the price; it neither shows its own form nor yet wishes to accept perceptibility.

For we do not perceive, at the time of the manifestation of distinct individuals such as the *śābaleya* cow which are mutually unmixed, any other inclusive [entity] different from them—such as a "neck-string" [is perceived] among living beings—since the cognition of a universal "śābaleya-ness" is unestablished. Therefore, how could we deceive ourselves by postulating something unseen? Thus, the reason (*hetu*) is not unestablished.

Nor does the suspicion of inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatā) fall beyond the scope of consideration, because its presence in the heterologue (vipakṣa) is not observed and its occurrence in the non-homologue (asapakṣa) is not found; thus, let there be no "common" inconclusiveness. However, the claim that the exclusion from the heterologue is doubtful due to the non-observation of an invariable connection (pratibandha) is a statement made by those whose intellects have not been sharpened by logical analysis. For such a suspicion is dispelled by the force of a subverting proof (bādhaka-pramāṇa) against the contrary [of the probandum].
For instance, when non-existence is the property to be proven (sādhya), existence is the counter-example (vipakṣa);

in that case, there must be the operation of perception (pratyakṣavṛtti). Because whatever has its capacity unimpaired and unobstructed necessarily exists at that time, just as a sprout does when the entire collection of its causes possesses complete strength.

And when there is the completeness of the eye and other factors, and the object to be seen is present, perception is knowledge whose causal capacity is unimpeded and complete; this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

Therefore, since the reason is excluded from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) by the apprehension of the contradictory, it is pervaded by the fitness for the conventional usage of "non-existent. Thus, because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established, the reason is not inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
This [position] is not correct.
However, because the contradiction [of the reason] is established by its opposition to the intended probandum, its forceful spread is utterly dispelled from afar.

Thus, when the matter at hand is established by a reason that is unstained by the blemish of doubts regarding fallacies such as "unestablished" (*asiddha*), it is proven that the universal (*sāmānya*) is non-existent. Enough with this excessively prolix and digressive discourse; therefore, we shall desist. [The text ends here.]
Nor is the universal, like the configuration of a thing, the defining characteristic of an individual.

Furthermore, the universal (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*) cannot consist of the nature of recurring and non-recurring phonemes and so forth, because that would entail the consequence of a cognition with a fixed appearance of the phonemes and so forth [belonging only to one of them]. If it is argued that this appearance belongs to the individual alone, then what else remains as the recurring form of the universal? Is there indeed anything else that persists apart from the phonemes and their configurations (*varṇasaṃsthāna*)? If it is argued that the two are perceived through a mutual blending—like milk and water—due to the power of inherence (*samavāya*), whereby the distinction between the universal and the individual is not manifested, then in that case, the form of neither the universal nor the particular is being grasped at all.

Since there would be no apprehension of these two either if their own nature were not apprehended, it follows that such a cognition is indeed without an objective basis (*nirālambana*). Thus, the ultimate reality has been set forth.
And is the universal (*sāmānya*) not well-established when it is being established by a cognition that is itself without an objective basis? R.

Therefore, this reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*) even due to the non-establishment of the qualificand; nor should it be considered contradictory (*viruddha*) because it exists in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*);
furthermore, the possibility of its being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) does not even deserve consideration.
For non-perception of the perceptible is pervaded by independence from the conventional usage of "non-existent.
If, despite being present, it did not function there, it would be dependent on something else;
therefore, being excluded from the counter-example because it is barred by what is incompatible with the pervader, it comes to rest in the conventional usage of "non-existent."

Therefore, since non-apprehension is pervaded by that conventional usage of "non-existent," how can there be any inconclusiveness? Consequently, this very point is established: he who perceives a sixth finger common to these five fingers clearly appearing in direct perception, perceives a horn upon his own head.
Thus it is pervaded;
in these five [realms] that are to be manifested.
He who perceives a sixth finger clearly in his direct perception of his own fingers,
is the one who sees a horn upon his own head.
It is maintained that this is the ultimate reality (paramārtha) of everything previously mentioned:
it does not reside in the five fingers appearing in direct perception.
The path does not abide within the five [aggregates], nor does it shine within the phenomena.
(S) Intro.
p.

A universal (sāmānya) does not appear as it exists in [external] objects; for in the cognition of a conceptual form, it is precisely those [individuals] that appear here with indistinct forms, and not the genus (jāti). Therefore, [the universal is not perceived].
Furthermore, these two—the perception and the sound—are the causes of the error of similarity;
thus, the general refutation of the proof [of a universal] has been established and set forth. S.
This is the work of the scholar Aśoka.
